'''William Richard Peltier''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada|FRSC]],<ref name=FRSC/> (born 1943), is university professor of physics at the [[University of Toronto]]. He is director of the Centre for Global Change Science,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.cgcs.utoronto.ca/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100323091645/http://www.cgcs.utoronto.ca/site3.aspx | archive-date=2010-03-23 | title=The University of Toronto Centre for Global Change Science}}</ref> past principal investigator of the Polar Climate Stability Network,<ref>[http://www.pcsn.ca/ Polar Climate Stability Network] on pcsn.ca</ref> and the scientific director of Canada's largest supercomputer centre, [[SciNet]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.scinethpc.ca/ | title=SciNet - High Performance Computing Consortium at the University of Toronto | website=www.scinethpc.ca}}</ref> He is a fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]], of the [[American Geophysical Union]], of the [[American Meteorological Society]], and of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]].

Peltier's research interests include: atmospheric and oceanic waves and turbulence, geophysical fluid dynamics, physics of the planetary interior, and planetary climate.

Peltier is notable for his seminal contributions to the understanding of the dynamics of the deep Earth, both concerning the nature of the mantle convection process and the circulation of the visco-elastic interior caused by the loading of the surface by continental scale ice sheet loads. His gravitationally self-consistent global theory of Ice-Earth-Ocean interactions has become widely employed internationally in the explanation of the changes of sea level that accompany both the growth and decay of grounded ice on the continents, both during the Late Quaternary era of Earth history and under modern global warming conditions. His models of the space-time variations of continental ice cover since the last maximum of glaciation are employed universally to provide the boundary conditions needed to enable modern coupled climate models to be employed to reconstruct past climate conditions. A most notable contribution to work of this kind has been his theory of the so-called [[Dansgaard–Oeschger event|Dansgaard-Oeschger]] millennial timescale oscillation of glacial climate.  He has been the primary contributor to the global reconstructions ICE-3G,<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1029/90JB01583|title=Ice-3G: A New Global Model of Late Pleistocene Deglaciation Based Upon Geophysical Predictions of Post-Glacial Relative Sea Level Change|year=1991|last1=Tushingham|first1=A. M.|last2=Peltier|first2=W. R.|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|volume=96|issue=B3|pages=4497–4523|bibcode=1991JGR....96.4497T}}</ref> ICE-4G,<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1126/science.265.5169.195|title=Ice Age Paleotopography|year=1994|last1=Peltier|first1=W. R.|journal=Science|volume=265|pages=195–201|pmid=17750657|issue=5169|bibcode = 1994Sci...265..195P |s2cid=29508590}}</ref> ICE-5G (VM2),<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.32.082503.144359|title=Global glacial isostasy and the surface of the ice-age Earth: the ICE-5G (VM2) Model and GRACE|year=2004|last1=Peltier|first1=W.R.|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|volume=32|pages=111–149|bibcode = 2004AREPS..32..111P }}</ref> and the most recent ICE-6G (VM5)model. These models are important for the quantification of [[post-glacial rebound]] and late [[Pleistocene]] to [[Holocene]] variations in [[sea level]].

== Career ==
While pursuing a college education in physics, Peltier supported himself by working for a geological firm, staking mineral claims in the [[Northwest Territories]]. He later said that the high density of black flies drove him to be a theorist.<ref name=Hall/> After getting his undergraduate degree at the [[University of British Columbia]], he went to the [[University of Toronto]] for his masters and Ph.D where he worked on the problem of [[mantle convection]] with Colin Hines as his graduate advisor.<ref name=Whitten/><ref name=cv/>

After Peltier graduated in 1971,<ref name=cv/> Hines arranged a postdoctoral fellowship for him at the [[Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences]] at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]]. There he met W. E. (Bill) Farrell, who was working on the deformation of an elastic Earth due to the tidally varying pressure of the oceans.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Baker|first1=Trevor F.|title=Earth Tides and Ocean Tide Loading – Bidston Observatory|url=http://www.bidstonobservatory.org.uk/earth-tides/|publisher=Bidston Observatory|accessdate=4 September 2017}}</ref> Farrell encouraged Peltier to work on a related problem, [[Post-glacial rebound|glacial isostatic adjustment]].<ref name=Whitten/>

''Glacial isostatic adjustment'' (GIA) is the response of the Earth to changing loads as glaciers advance and retreat. On time scales of hundreds of thousand of years, Earth's [[lithosphere]] behaves as if it is floating on the [[Earth's mantle|mantle]], and given enough time it achieves a state of [[isostasy]] where denser material sinks and lighter material rises to balance the gravitational load. However, when a large load such as a [[glacier]] is added, it presses the lithosphere down; and when it melts away, the lithosphere rises, a phenomenon known as [[post-glacial rebound]]. After the most recent [[ice age]], some parts of [[Canada]] and [[Scandinavia]] have rebounded by nearly 300 meters and are still rising (relative to [[sea level]]) at several millimeters per year.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Gornitz|first1=Vivien|title=Rising seas past, present, future|date=2013|publisher=Columbia University Press|location=New York|isbn=9780231519205}}</ref>{{rp|43&ndash;44}} The rate of adjustment is slow because the Earth's mantle has a high [[viscosity]]. Peltier was already aware from his doctoral work that models of mantle convection required a good estimate of viscosity, and he realized that this could be obtained from an analysis of GIA.<ref name=Whitten/> Modeling the Earth as a [[Maxwell material|Maxwell solid]], an incompressible material with both viscosity and elasticity, he showed that a ''correspondence principle'' could be used to reduce the viscoelastic problem to the simpler elastic problem.<ref>{{cite book|first1=N. M.|last1=Ribe|chapter= 4. Analytical Approaches to Mantle Dynamics|editor-last1=Bercovici|editor-first1=David|title=Mantle Dynamics: Treatise on Geophysics|date=2010|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9780444535801|page=196}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Sabadini,...|first1=Roberto|last2=Vermeersen|first2=Bert|title=Global dynamics of the earth applications of normal mode relaxation theory to solid-earth geophysics|date=2004|publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers|location=Dordrecht|isbn=9781402012686|page=3}}</ref>

During this period, Peltier also worked on the [[geophysical fluid dynamics]] of the atmosphere, studying [[internal wave]]s in the [[jet stream]] and oceanic [[boundary current]]s.<ref name=Whitten/> In a 1976 paper with Hines he proposed monitoring the [[ionosphere]] to detect [[tsunami]]s;<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Peltier|first1=W. R.|last2=Hines|first2=C. O.|title=On the possible detection of tsunamis by a monitoring of the ionosphere|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|date=20 April 1976|volume=81|issue=12|pages=1995–2000|doi=10.1029/JC081i012p01995}}</ref> thirty years later, when [[global positioning system|GPS systems]] became available, there was a resurgence of interest in this idea.<ref name=Whitten/>

Aside from visiting appointments and [[sabbatical]]s, Peltier has spent his entire career at the University of Toronto (U of T).<ref name=Whitten/> In 1977, he was granted tenure, in 1979 he became a full professor, and in 1993 he was appointed University Professor. This is the highest academic title at U of T, held by at most 2 percent of tenured faculty.<ref>{{cite web|title=Current University Professors|url=http://www.provost.utoronto.ca/awards/uprofessors/current-professors.htm|website=Office of the Vice-President & Provost|publisher=University of Toronto|accessdate=4 September 2017|language=en}}</ref> He has had sabbaticals at the [[University of Cambridge]], the [[National Center for Atmospheric Research]] in Boulder, and the [[Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris]].<ref name=Whitten/>

==Publications==
Peltier has published over 280 peer-reviewed papers for a total of over 32,000 citations and an h-index of 87.<ref name=cv/><ref>{{cite web|title=W.R. Peltier|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=yes-VnIAAAAJ&hl=en|website=Google Scholar Citations|accessdate=3 September 2017}}</ref> In 2001, ''Science Watch'' analyzed citation data from ''Essential Science Indicators'' and found that Peltier was the fifth most cited researcher in the geosciences for 1991 to 2001.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The greatest research on Earth|journal=Science Watch|date=November–December 2001|volume=12|issue=6|url=http://www.sciencewatch.com:80/nov-dec2001/sw_nov-dec2001_page1.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030104175954/http://www.sciencewatch.com:80/nov-dec2001/sw_nov-dec2001_page1.htm|archive-date=4 January 2003}}</ref>
Some of his papers are:
*{{cite journal|last1=Peltier|first1=W. R.|title=The impulse response of a Maxwell Earth|journal=Reviews of Geophysics|date=1974|volume=12|issue=4|pages=649|doi=10.1029/RG012i004p00649}}
*{{cite journal|last1=Peltier|first1=W. R.|last2=Andrews|first2=J. T.|title=Glacial-Isostatic Adjustment-I. The Forward Problem|journal=Geophysical Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society|date=2 April 2007|volume=46|issue=3|pages=605–646|doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.1976.tb01251.x}}
*{{cite journal|last1=Tushingham|first1=A. M.|last2=Peltier|first2=W. R.|title=Ice-3G: A new global model of Late Pleistocene deglaciation based upon geophysical predictions of post-glacial relative sea level change|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth|date=10 March 1991|volume=96|issue=B3|pages=4497–4523|doi=10.1029/90JB01583|bibcode=1991JGR....96.4497T }}
*{{cite journal|last1=Peltier|first1=W. Richard|title=Ice age paleotopography|journal=Science|date=8 July 1994|volume=265|issue=5169|pages=195&ndash;201|doi=10.1126/science.265.5169.195 |jstor=2884168|pmid=17750657 |bibcode=1994Sci...265..195P |s2cid=29508590 }}
*{{cite journal|last1=Peltier|first1=W.R.|title=Global glacial isostasy and the surface of the ice-age Earth: the ICE-5G (VM2) model and GRACE|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|date=19 May 2004|volume=32|issue=1|pages=111–149|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.32.082503.144359|bibcode=2004AREPS..32..111P }}
*{{cite journal|last1=Peltier|first1=W.R.|last2=Fairbanks|first2=R.G.|title=Global glacial ice volume and Last Glacial Maximum duration from an extended Barbados sea level record|journal=Quaternary Science Reviews|date=December 2006|volume=25|issue=23–24|pages=3322–3337|doi=10.1016/j.quascirev.2006.04.010}}
*{{cite journal|last1=Shackleton|first1=N. J.|last2=Berger|first2=A.|last3=Peltier|first3=W.
